hero.title: Coursera Specialization Structure
hero.subtitle: A Specialization is a set of related courses, each built to stand on its own and be reused.
hero.hint: Click any element below to learn more about it.

specialization.label: SPECIALIZATION
specialization.rail: A set of related courses that together help learners develop mastery in one subject.
specialization.definition: A series of related, in-depth courses that help learners develop mastery in a high-demand subject.
specialization.outcome: Learners who complete every course earn a Specialization Certificate. In some cases it can count toward an accredited degree on Coursera.

detail.title: Specialization
body: A Specialization is a series of related, in-depth courses that help learners develop mastery in a high-demand subject. Specializations include projects — hands-on assessments with real-world applications.
Learners who complete an entire Specialization earn a Specialization Certificate. In some cases, that certificate counts toward earning an accredited degree on Coursera.
Design it as a coherent set rather than a fixed path. Learners can enroll in any course in any order, and a well-built course may later be reused in a different Specialization.
tips: Define the subject mastery the whole set adds up to before planning individual courses.
Plan for 3–4 courses and 12–32 hours of total learner time.
Every course must work for someone who takes only that one course.
Plan where the hands-on project(s) live early; they're expected, not optional.

courses.label: COURSES
courses.rail: Each course teaches its own focused set of learning objectives. Courses are not chapters — any one of them may be reused in another Specialization later.

callout.title: Design for reuse, not for sequence
callout.body: Avoid building courses that depend on each other. Don't reference other courses by name or number, and don't assume a learner has taken them. Each course should make sense on its own so it can be recombined into a different Specialization without rewriting.

detail.title: Course
body: Courses give learners access to instructional videos, assessments, and other learning content. Learners who pay for and complete a course earn a shareable course certificate that recognizes their accomplishment.
Each course carries its own focused set of 2–4 learning objectives. Those objectives — not its position in a sequence — are what define the course.
Build every course as a self-contained unit. Coursera lets anyone enroll in any course at any time, and your team may want to reuse this course in a different Specialization later.
tips: Name the course for its skill or subject, not for a number.
Never write "as you saw in Course 1" — name the concept or skill instead.
State needed background as a skill, not as another course a learner should have taken.
Target 2–4 learning objectives, 3–4 modules, and 2–8 hours of learning.

modules.label: MODULES
modules.rail: A module is the fundamental container of content within a course. Modules make up the course structure and schedule.
modules.note: Modules don't have to follow a fixed arc. Organize each one around a coherent topic or skill, not around its position in the course.

cards.title: Module
cards.role: A coherent topic or skill within the course.

cards.role: A coherent topic or skill within the course.

detail.title: Module
body: A module acts as the fundamental container of content within a course. Modules make up the overall course structure and schedule. On Coursera, learners complete modules at their own pace based on personalized deadlines that reflect their own learning goals.
Each module carries 2–4 learning objectives and at least one graded assessment that measures whether those objectives were met.
Modules do not need to follow a foundational-to-advanced arc. Build each one around a topic that holds together on its own.
tips: Name the module for its topic or skill — Coursera adds the number.
Every module needs at least one graded assessment tied to its own objectives.
Include ungraded practice before the graded assessment.
Vary the asset types; avoid several of the same format in a row.

lessons.label: LESSONS
lessons.rail: Lessons are an optional way to group related content inside a module.
lessons.definition: Lessons group concepts within a module. They're optional — use them when a module has enough content that grouping helps learners navigate it.

detail.title: Lesson
body: A lesson is an optional grouping layer inside a module. Lessons let you cluster related items so a long module is easier for learners to navigate.
You don't have to use lessons. A module with only a handful of items usually reads better without them.
tips: Group by idea, not by format — don't make a "videos" lesson and a "readings" lesson.
Start a new lesson when the sub-topic changes or a learner would naturally pause.
If a module only has a few items, skip lessons entirely.

assets.label: LEARNING ASSETS
assets.rail: Modules and lessons contain a mix of assets that teach, let learners practice, and assess what they've learned.
assets.alsoAvailable: Also available: in-video questions, discussion prompts, peer review assignments, programming assignments, in-browser coding, and third-party plugins.

cards.title: Videos
cards.short: Introduce and teach a course topic.

detail.title: Video item
body: Videos introduce and teach a course topic. Each video item should be short and focused.
tips: Ideally three to nine minutes in length.
One idea per video — not a recorded lecture cut into pieces.
In-video questions (IVQs) can be embedded to pause the video and prompt a quick check.
Provide the recording, slide deck, or an approved production placeholder.

cards.title: Readings
cards.short: Articles or guides that deepen understanding.

detail.title: Reading
body: Learner-facing text used to explain, extend, or provide reference material. Best for anything learners will want to scan, search, or return to later.
tips: Provide the complete text, not an outline.
Include links, images, alt text, and any needed permissions.
Good for reference material, worked examples, and step-by-step instructions.

cards.title: Coach Dialogue
cards.short: AI-driven conversations that reflect and apply.

detail.title: Coach Dialogue
body: Dialogue items are course activities that enable authors to create AI-driven discussions simulating interactions with a live instructor. These items lead learners through structured, text-based conversations designed to achieve specific learning objectives.

In a live Dialogue, the AI guide (Coursera Coach) helps learners think critically and apply course concepts to real-world situations by asking adaptive, open-ended questions. Dialogues are tailored to each learner and provide personalized feedback.
tips: Write the coach goal: what should the learner think through, decide, or produce?
Provide an opening question, 2–4 follow-up areas, and a closing reflection.
Best for reflection, applying ideas to the learner's own context, or rehearsing a decision.
Ungraded unless you specify otherwise.

detail.title: Hands-on practice
body: Activities where learners try the skill directly. On Coursera this can be an ungraded activity, a Coursera Lab, in-browser coding, or an embedded third-party plugin.
In-browser coding lets learners complete hands-on work without leaving Coursera or setting up a local environment — executable code blocks, programming assignments, and Coursera Labs.
tips: Provide the activity plus step-by-step learner instructions and setup details.
Labs need notebooks/files plus environment details — confirm feasibility early.
No stakes. This is where learners get to fail safely.

cards.title: Practice Quiz
cards.short: Low-stakes quiz for practice and self-check.

detail.title: Practice assessment
body: Practice assessments are optional and ungraded, and they don't count toward a learner's final course grade. They support learning by helping learners self-assess their progress and master skills they've learned.
They also give you a chance to provide learners with meaningful feedback.
tips: Provide every question, the correct answers, and feedback for both correct and incorrect responses.
Should rehearse the same thinking the graded assessment will ask for.
Optional and ungraded — use them generously.

cards.title: Graded Assessment
cards.short: Measures mastery of the module's objectives.

detail.title: Graded assessment
body: Graded assessments give learners a chance to apply what they've learned. They measure a learner's level of mastery and progress toward a learning objective. Graded assessments are required and count toward a learner's final course grade.
Every module needs at least one.
tips: Must map to the module's stated learning objectives.
A 10-question auto-graded quiz with answer-specific feedback is the common default.
Other formats exist — peer review, programming assignments — but check which satisfy the per-module requirement.
Write feedback for incorrect answers, not just correct ones.

comparison.title: How this differs from a for-credit course
comparison.intro: Most of the surprises in a first Coursera build come from assumptions carried over from semester teaching.

rows.coursera: No schedule. Learners start any day and work at their own pace on personalized deadlines.

rows.credit: You're in the room; you can adjust live
rows.coursera: Fully asynchronous. Everything a learner needs has to already be in the course.
Anyone can enroll in any course, in any order. Prerequisites are stated, not enforced.

rows.credit: Courses build on each other within a program
rows.coursera: Courses are modular. A course may be reused in a different Specialization.
2–8 hours of learning per course; 12–32 hours across the whole Specialization.
Working adults worldwide, widely varied backgrounds, mostly self-motivated.
Mostly auto-graded. At least one graded assessment per module.

rows.credit: Grades and tuition keep students enrolled
rows.coursera: Nothing holds anyone. Every module has to earn the next click.

completion.title: Certificates
completion.body: Learners who complete a single course earn a shareable course certificate. Learners who complete every course in the Specialization earn a Specialization Certificate — which in some cases counts toward an accredited degree on Coursera.

handoff.title: Ready to plan yours?
handoff.body: The template is the blank version of everything above — no guidance, just the fields your design team needs. Come back here any time you want a refresher.
